conversion_quality.interpretation: Measures conversion/extraction quality, not whether the source literature itself is scientifically correct.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: Traditional scientific articles are ambiguous, incomplete, and difficult for automated systems to process, motivating a machine-readable approach for packaging research artefacts and their metadata.

evidence_for.rationale: Authors' own framing in the Introduction directly motivates the need addressed by RO-Crate.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Authors state that experience with prior bundling/packaging approaches showed greater emphasis on artefact interconnection was needed and that previous Research Object implementations require a large technology stack inaccessible to typical users.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: RO-Crate is introduced as an open, community-driven, lightweight approach to packaging research artefacts and their metadata in a machine-readable manner using Schema.org annotations in JSON-LD.

evidence_for.rationale: Comparison with prior Wf4Ever RO model motivates RO-Crate's simpler positioning that the abstract states.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Prior Research Object framework (Wf4Ever) is cited as harder to adopt due to its reliance on multiple overlapping vocabularies and Semantic Web development choices, motivating the simpler RO-Crate approach.

evidence_for.rationale: Documented community membership and engagement supports the 'open, community-driven' framing of RO-Crate.
evidence_for.evidence_text: RO-Crate community comprised more than 50 members at time of writing (October 2021), with monthly calls, Slack channel, mailing list, and engagement with EU projects (ELIXIR, EOSC-Life, FAIRplus, BY-COVID).

claim_readouts.assertion_text: RO-Crate is designed around four explicit principles: conceptual simplicity for developers, strong easy tooling, an opinionated guide of current best practices, and adoption of de-facto Web standards.

evidence_for.rationale: Direct enumeration of the four design principles in the text of Section 2 supports the stated principles claim.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Authors explicitly state the four design principles of RO-Crate as: conceptually simple, strong easy tooling, opinionated best-practice guide, and adoption of de-facto Web standards.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: RO-Crate's underlying data structure, although conceptually a graph, is representable as a depth-limited tree, and this boundedness separates Data Entities (hasPart) from external Contextual Entities (mentions).

evidence_for.rationale: Appendix A FOL formalisation provides the analytical basis for the depth-limited tree / boundedness claim.
evidence_for.evidence_text: First-Order Logic formalisation of RO-Crate in Appendix A establishes that RO-Crate is representable as a depth-limited tree with bounded structure, and supports forward-chained production rules to generate JSON-LD.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: RO-Crate has been adopted across diverse domains - bioinformatics workflows (WorkflowHub), regulatory science (BCO RO-Crate), cultural heritage (Modern PARADISEC), data management plans, and institutional repositories (Harvard Data Commons) - through domain-specific profiles.

evidence_for.rationale: WorkflowHub adoption is one of the principal cross-domain adoptions cited by the cross-domain-adoption claim.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Documented use of RO-Crate at WorkflowHub - a cross-domain workflow registry supported by ELIXIR and EOSC-Life - including dedicated Workflow RO-Crate, Workflow Run, and Workflow Testing profiles. Co-development informed the Bioschemas ComputationalWorkflow profile.

evidence_for.rationale: BCO RO-Crate is the explicit regulatory-science use case for cross-domain adoption.
evidence_for.evidence_text: BCO RO-Crate, part of the BioCompute Object user guides, defines a profile for wrapping BCO/workflow regulatory submissions inside an RO-Crate (illustrated in Fig. 3).

evidence_for.rationale: PARADISEC is one of the digital-humanities adoption cases enumerated.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Modern PARADISEC demonstrator captures more than 500,000 files documenting endangered languages in RO-Crates over OCFL, exposing them through a Web portal independent of the original platform.

evidence_for.rationale: Harvard Data Commons adoption is a documented institutional use case for RO-Crate.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Harvard Data Commons, integrating Harvard Research Computing with Harvard Dataverse (over 120K datasets, 1.3M files), is adopting RO-Crate to make multiple institutional research artefacts FAIR (illustrated in Fig. 4).

evidence_for.rationale: Cross-language, cross-platform tool inventory demonstrates breadth of adoption underpinning the multi-domain claim.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Table 1 enumerates 15+ RO-Crate tools across multiple programming languages (Python, JavaScript, Ruby, Java, PHP) and platforms, used by developers, data managers, and end users.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: WorkflowHub adopted RO-Crate as the packaging mechanism for cross-domain workflows, marking up workflow language and constituent files, and this co-development helped shape both the Bioschemas Computational Workflow profile and the RO-Crate 1.1 workflows specification.

evidence_for.rationale: Section 4.1 details WorkflowHub's adoption and the co-development with Bioschemas, directly supporting the assertion.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Documented use of RO-Crate at WorkflowHub - a cross-domain workflow registry supported by ELIXIR and EOSC-Life - including dedicated Workflow RO-Crate, Workflow Run, and Workflow Testing profiles. Co-development informed the Bioschemas ComputationalWorkflow profile.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: The Modern PARADISEC demonstrator uses RO-Crate to capture metadata of more than 500,000 endangered-language items in a portable, platform-independent way that supports long-term preservation and SPARQL-queryable corpora.

evidence_for.rationale: The PARADISEC scale numbers and reuse pattern directly support the cultural-heritage adoption claim.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Modern PARADISEC demonstrator captures more than 500,000 files documenting endangered languages in RO-Crates over OCFL, exposing them through a Web portal independent of the original platform.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: RO-Crate can serve as a Metadata FDO and provide a predictable, extensible serialisation of structured metadata for FAIR Digital Object ecosystems.

evidence_for.rationale: Authors explicitly argue RO-Crate fits within FDO ecosystems while noting FDO's broader requirements.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Authors note that the goal of FDO is broader than RO-Crate, requiring PIDs for every element and active operations, but argue a FAIR-profiled RO-Crate fits within an FDO ecosystem.

mixed_or_inconclusive.rationale: While FDO compatibility is argued, the authors acknowledge that the FDO goal is broader, qualifying any strong RO-Crate-as-Metadata-FDO claim.
mixed_or_inconclusive.evidence_text: Authors note that the goal of FDO is broader than RO-Crate, requiring PIDs for every element and active operations, but argue a FAIR-profiled RO-Crate fits within an FDO ecosystem.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: RO-Crate is not merely a packaging container but functions as a multimodal scholarly knowledge graph that helps FAIRify and combine metadata of existing resources.

evidence_for.rationale: The Linked-Data and Schema.org-based design enumerated in the principles underpins the 'knowledge graph' conclusion.
evidence_for.evidence_text: Authors explicitly state the four design principles of RO-Crate as: conceptually simple, strong easy tooling, opinionated best-practice guide, and adoption of de-facto Web standards.

claim_readouts.assertion_text: There is an unresolved tradeoff between flexibility (richness/applicability) and strictness (ease of producing and consuming) of metadata models, and RO-Crate addresses this by combining a flexible core with domain-specific profiles.
